newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: FOCUS-S.Korea's banks decide to bail out Kia Group.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-S.Korea's banks decide to bail out Kia Group.

text.p: South Korean banks stepped in on Tuesday to rescue the Kia Group, the country's eighth largest business conglomerate, whose carmaking flagship has been battered by slumping sales.
Creditors selected 18 of Kia's 38 affiliates for rescue, according to a statement from the Korea First Bank, the group's biggest creditor.
It was the third rescue of a South Korean firm by a consortium of banks and financial institutions in three months.

"The creditor's decision was unexpected because we have tried our best to meet our loan payments, but the decision will keep our bank accounts open and there will be no damage to our customers," said Ahn Suk-woo, group spokesman.
He said the rescue plan would be in effect for two months.
The Kia Group had total debts of 9.54 trillion won ($10.7 billion) at the end of May, according to the Korea Federation of Banks.
Like other car manufacturers, Kia has been struggling due to a severe industry downturn. It had sought to stay afloat by cutting jobs and shedding assets.
Vehicle sales in the first half of this year dropped to 160,000 from 220,000 a year earlier.
Kia's woes were compounded by persistent rumours over its financial health that savaged the share prices of its listed affiliates, including Kia Motors, one of the country's top three automakers.
Kia Motors' largest single shareholder is U.S. auto giant Ford Motor Co with a 16.9 percent holding.
A challenge by newcomer Samsung Motors, rumoured to be interested in buying Kia Motors as a short-cut into the industry's top ranks, added to a sense of crisis.

The bail-out reflects concern by authorities to prevent a domino-effect of bankruptcies following the country's biggest ever corporate failure in January when Hanbo Steel collapsed under 6.6 trillion won in debt.
Also included in the bail-out plan are Asia Motors, Kia Steel, Kisan, Kia Precision, Kia Service and 12 other unlisted units.
A Korea First Bank statement blamed the deteriorating business performances of major Kia units for the crisis and said creditors would meet on July 30 to work out details of the package.
In the previous two bail-outs of the Jinro and Dainong Groups, the family owners were required to give up management control to creditors in return for funds.
To head off tight liquidity in the short-term money markets, the Bank of Korea said it would release one trillion won through repurchase agreements.
A central bank official, who declined to be identified, said Kia sought the rescue to stave off debt repayment defaults.
He noted that some commercial banks were facing difficulties meeting reserve requirements.
The Korea Stock Exchange halted trading in all six listed Kia shares for the afternoon session. Trading would resume on Wednesday, an exchange official said.

News of the rescue sent share prices tumbling on the exchange. The leading index plunged by more than two percent but later recovered to end the day down 1.23 percent, or 9.40 points, to 755.05 points.
"Kia problems sparked across-the-board selling," said Lee Hee-myong at Samsung Securities.
"The impact for the economy will be enormous, if a business entity with nine trillion won liabilities fails," Kim Myong-Ho at Hyundai Securities said.

In an interview with Reuters last week, Kia chairman Kim Sun-hong, said he believed the group was on the road to recovery following new harmony between labour and management that had led to agreements on a restructuring.
Kim said the introduction of five new models this year would also boost the company's fortunes.
The group is seeking to cut Kia Motors' 20,000-strong workforce by 10 percent. Asia Motors union has agreed to a reduction of 1,447 jobs from 9,200.
The group had announced it would sell some 795 billion won worth of idle assets.
This month Kia creditors agreed to supply $300 million in export loans to the group.
